title: OOP & Design Patterns (All 23 GoF)
description: All 23 Gang of Four patterns (Creational, Structural, Behavioral) with JS/TS code examples + SOLID deep dive. Maps to Turing T1 MCQ, T3 Live, T4 FDE.

options: Open/Closed Principle
Single Responsibility Principle
Liskov Substitution Principle
Dependency Inversion Principle
questions.explanation: UserService has 3 reasons to change: user retrieval logic, email sending, and logging. SRP says a class should have only one reason to change. Fix: split into UserRepository, EmailService, ActivityLogger.

questions.prompt: The Open/Closed Principle states code should be open for __ and closed for __.
options: modification; extension
extension; modification
testing; deployment
inheritance; composition
questions.explanation: OCP: open for extension (new behaviour via new classes or interfaces), closed for modification (existing code shouldn't change). Classic implementation: Strategy pattern, template method, polymorphism.

questions.prompt: Liskov Substitution Principle violation: a `Square` extends `Rectangle` and overrides `setWidth` to also set `setHeight`. The violation is:
options: Square has extra methods Rectangle doesn't
Substituting Square for Rectangle breaks code that changes width independently of height
Square is immutable but Rectangle is mutable
Square overrides a method it shouldn't
questions.explanation: Code like `r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(10); assert(r.area() == 50)` passes for Rectangle but fails for Square (area = 100). LSP: subtype must be substitutable for its base type without changing program correctness.

questions.prompt: Interface Segregation Principle applied: instead of one fat `IWorker` interface with `work()`, `eat()`, `sleep()`, you should:
options: Add default implementations for unused methods
Split into IWorkable, IFeedable, ISleepable so classes only implement what they need
Make all methods optional using TypeScript's Partial<T>
Use a single abstract class with all methods
questions.explanation: ISP: no class should be forced to depend on methods it doesn't use. A Robot implements IWorkable but shouldn't implement IFeedable. Split interfaces keep implementations lean and tests focused.

questions.prompt: Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level modules should depend on __, not on __.
options: abstractions; concrete implementations
concrete implementations; abstractions
interfaces; classes
functions; objects
questions.explanation: DIP: both high-level (business logic) and low-level (infrastructure) modules should depend on abstractions (interfaces). This enables swapping implementations without changing business logic. Achieved via constructor injection.

questions.prompt: Singleton pattern ensures a class has exactly one instance. The thread-safety issue in lazy initialization is solved in JS/TS by:
options: Using a mutex lock around the constructor
Module-level singleton (Node's module cache ensures single evaluation per process)
Double-checked locking pattern
Using WeakMap to store instances
questions.explanation: In Node.js, `require()` / ES module `import` caches the module after first execution. Exporting a single instance at module level is inherently singleton — the module is only evaluated once. No explicit locking needed unlike Java.

questions.prompt: Factory Method vs Abstract Factory: the key difference is:
options: Factory Method creates one product; Abstract Factory creates families of related products
Abstract Factory is always faster
Factory Method uses inheritance; Abstract Factory uses composition only
They are identical — just different names
questions.explanation: Factory Method: one interface, one product type, subclasses decide which class to instantiate. Abstract Factory: creates families of related objects (e.g., Button+Dialog for Win vs Mac) without specifying concrete classes.

questions.prompt: Builder pattern is most appropriate when:
options: A class has a single optional field
Construction of an object requires many steps or optional parameters, and the same construction process should produce different representations
You need to clone an existing object cheaply
You want to control the number of instances
questions.explanation: Builder separates construction from representation. Classic: building a complex HTTP request, a SQL query, or a UI component with many optional configurations. Avoids telescoping constructor anti-pattern.

questions.prompt: Prototype pattern in JavaScript is natural because:
options: JavaScript is prototype-based — every object can serve as a prototype via Object.create() or structuredClone()
JavaScript has no classes so Prototype is the only creational option
JavaScript's `new` keyword implements Prototype automatically
Prototype is the fastest creational pattern in all languages
questions.explanation: Prototype creates new objects by cloning existing ones. In JS, Object.create(proto) or structuredClone(obj) implement this. Useful when object initialization is expensive (e.g., DB-loaded config objects).

questions.prompt: Adapter pattern purpose:
options: Simplifies a complex subsystem's interface
Makes incompatible interfaces work together by wrapping one in a class that translates calls
Adds new behaviour to an object without modifying its class
Controls access to another object
questions.explanation: Adapter wraps an existing class (Adaptee) to make it compatible with a Target interface. Example: wrapping a 3rd-party payment library (Stripe) behind your own IPaymentGateway interface so swapping providers requires only one new Adapter.

questions.prompt: Decorator pattern vs Inheritance for adding behaviour: decorators are preferred when:
options: You need to add behaviour at compile time only
You need to add or combine behaviours at runtime without modifying the original class or creating a subclass explosion
Behaviour can't be described as an interface
You're working in a class-based OOP language only
questions.explanation: Inheritance causes class explosion (LoggedUserService, CachedUserService, CachedLoggedUserService...). Decorator wraps objects at runtime and can be stacked. Node.js middleware pipeline is a real-world Decorator.

questions.prompt: Facade pattern in software: the express app's `app.use(cors()).use(json()).use(router)` is an example because:
options: It uses the Decorator pattern to add middleware
app.use() provides a simple interface that hides the complex request processing pipeline underneath
It's an Observer with multiple subscribers
It uses the Command pattern to queue middleware
questions.explanation: Facade provides a simple interface to a complex subsystem. The user calls app.use() without knowing how the middleware chain, request lifecycle, or error propagation work internally. Same applies to SDK wrappers around complex APIs.

questions.prompt: Proxy pattern has three main uses: virtual proxy (lazy loading), protection proxy (access control), and remote proxy. Which is most common in Node.js backends?
options: Remote proxy — using JavaScript Proxy to intercept property access for caching or validation
Virtual proxy — loading heavy resources only on demand
Protection proxy — wrapping service calls with auth checks
All three are equally common
questions.explanation: Protection proxies wrapping service calls with auth/rate-limiting checks are extremely common. But JavaScript's built-in `Proxy` object most directly implements the virtual/validation proxy. Answer (c) is the most architecturally impactful use in backend services.

questions.prompt: Composite pattern is used when you need to treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly. Classic example:
options: A filesystem where files and directories share the same interface (both have name, size, delete)
A strategy pattern with multiple algorithms
A chain of middleware handlers
A factory that creates different types of nodes
questions.explanation: Composite defines a tree structure of objects all sharing one Component interface. Both Leaf (File) and Composite (Directory) implement the same interface. Client code calls `component.getSize()` without knowing if it's a file or nested directory.

questions.prompt: Flyweight pattern reduces memory usage by sharing common state. In a text editor rendering 10,000 characters, Flyweight:
options: Creates one object per unique character type (glyph), sharing intrinsic state (font, style) — each rendered char only stores its extrinsic position
Caches the last 100 character renders
Renders all characters in one batch draw call
Compresses the character buffer using run-length encoding
questions.explanation: Flyweight separates intrinsic (shared: glyph shape, font) from extrinsic (unique: position, colour). 10,000 chars of 52 types → 52 Flyweight objects instead of 10,000. Same pattern used in game engines for particles/bullets.

questions.prompt: Bridge pattern separates abstraction from implementation so they can vary independently. Difference from Adapter:
options: Adapter makes existing incompatible classes work together (retrofit); Bridge is designed upfront to allow both sides to evolve independently
Bridge is always bidirectional; Adapter is one-way
They are functionally identical — just different intent
Bridge requires an interface; Adapter works only with concrete classes
questions.explanation: Adapter = retrofit (makes two incompatible things work). Bridge = design upfront (defines two independent hierarchies: e.g., Shape abstraction + Renderer implementation). You can add Shapes or Renderers independently without touching the other side.

questions.prompt: Observer pattern: when an event emitter in Node.js fires 'data', all listeners are called. The emitter is the __ and listeners are the __.
options: Observer; Subject
Subject; Observer
Publisher; Consumer
Producer; Subscriber
questions.explanation: Observer (GoF): Subject maintains a list of Observers and notifies them on state change. EventEmitter is the Subject; `.on('data', fn)` registers fn as an Observer. Publisher/Subscriber is a variation via a message broker.

questions.prompt: Strategy pattern vs State pattern: the key difference is:
options: Strategy: client chooses algorithm at runtime; State: object changes its behaviour automatically based on internal state transitions
State: client switches strategies; Strategy: internal state machine decides
They are identical — just different naming conventions
Strategy uses interfaces; State uses abstract classes
questions.explanation: Strategy: client explicitly sets which algorithm to use (e.g., choose sorting algorithm). State: the object's behaviour changes as its internal state changes (e.g., traffic light — Red/Green/Yellow states each know their next state). State transitions are internal.

questions.prompt: Command pattern encapsulates a request as an object. This enables:
options: Queuing operations, logging, undo/redo — because commands are first-class objects that can be stored and replayed
Faster request processing via memoization
Distributing requests across multiple threads
All of the above
questions.explanation: Command decouples sender from receiver. Storing Command objects enables: undo/redo (reverse the command), queuing (send to a message queue), logging (replay on crash recovery), and macro recording (batch of commands). HTTP request objects are a real-world Command.

questions.prompt: Chain of Responsibility: an HTTP request passes through authentication → authorization → rate limiting → logging middleware. Each handler:
options: Processes the request and then passes it to the next handler, or short-circuits by returning early
All handlers always run in parallel
Only the first matching handler runs
Handlers vote; majority decides if request proceeds
questions.explanation: CoR: each handler decides to process and pass the request, or stop the chain (short-circuit). Express.js middleware (`next()` vs returning without calling `next`) is CoR. Each handler doesn't know which handler comes next.

questions.prompt: Template Method pattern: a base class defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a method, deferring some steps to subclasses. TypeScript example: abstract `DataProcessor` with `process()` calling `readData()` + `transformData()` + `writeData()`. The Template Method is:
options: readData()
transformData()
process()
writeData()
questions.explanation: `process()` is the Template Method — it defines the invariant algorithm skeleton. The abstract `readData()`, `transformData()`, `writeData()` are 'hooks' that subclasses override. The overall sequence never changes; only the hook implementations vary.

questions.prompt: Iterator pattern in JavaScript: which built-in mechanism implements the Iterator protocol?
options: Array.forEach()
Symbol.iterator / for...of loops
Array.map()
Object.keys()
questions.explanation: JS Iterator protocol: an object is iterable if it has `[Symbol.iterator]()` returning an object with `.next()` returning `{value, done}`. `for...of`, spread operator, and destructuring all use this. Custom iterators (for paginated DB cursors, lazy ranges) implement this protocol.

questions.prompt: Mediator pattern reduces chaos in systems where many objects communicate with each other. Instead of O(n²) connections:
options: Each object communicates only through a central Mediator — O(n) connections total
Objects are grouped into pairs that communicate directly
A shared event bus replaces the mediator
Objects broadcast; others filter
questions.explanation: Mediator: all objects reference one Mediator object. They send messages to the mediator; it routes to the right recipient. Air traffic control (planes ↔ ATC ↔ planes rather than plane-to-plane). Note: Event Bus can implement Mediator but is architecturally different (decentralised).

questions.prompt: Memento pattern saves and restores an object's state without exposing internals. A text editor's Ctrl+Z (undo) uses Memento. The three roles are:
options: Originator (editor state), Memento (snapshot object), Caretaker (undo history stack)
Producer, Snapshot, Consumer
Source, Delta, Target
Object, Clone, Repository
questions.explanation: Originator creates snapshots (Mementos) of its own internal state. Caretaker (history stack) stores and manages Mementos. Restoration: Caretaker passes Memento back to Originator which restores itself. Originator's internal state is never exposed to Caretaker.

questions.prompt: Visitor pattern lets you add operations to objects without modifying their classes. Trade-off:
options: Easy to add new element types; hard to add new operations
Easy to add new operations; hard to add new element types
Both are equally easy to extend
Visitor only works with immutable data structures
questions.explanation: Adding a new Visitor (operation) requires only a new Visitor class — no change to element classes. But adding a new element type requires updating every existing Visitor. Contrast with normal OOP: easy to add element types, hard to add new operations without modifying existing classes.

questions.prompt: Interpreter pattern interprets sentences in a language. Where is it commonly used in modern software?
options: HTTP request routing
Regular expressions, SQL query parsers, and rule engines
Sorting algorithms
Concurrency control
questions.explanation: Interpreter defines a grammar and an interpreter for it. Regex engines, SQL parsers, expression evaluators (math formula engines), and DSL rule engines all implement Interpreter. Each grammar rule is a class with an `interpret()` method.

questions.prompt: Composition over inheritance principle: why is it usually preferred?
options: Composition is always faster than inheritance at runtime
Composition avoids fragile base class problem, allows behaviour mixing at runtime, and doesn't couple objects to deep inheritance trees
Composition is easier to write
Inheritance breaks encapsulation in all languages
questions.explanation: Fragile base class: a change to a superclass can break all subclasses. Deep inheritance makes code hard to reason about. Composition (has-a) instead of inheritance (is-a) lets you mix behaviours, swap implementations, and test in isolation. GoF explicitly recommends 'favour composition over inheritance'.

questions.prompt: The 'Law of Demeter' (principle of least knowledge) says a method should only talk to:
options: Its direct collaborators: itself, its parameters, objects it creates, and its direct fields — not objects returned by calling methods on those objects
Any object in the same module
Only pure functions
Objects registered in a service locator
questions.explanation: LoD: `user.getAddress().getCity().getZip()` violates LoD — you're calling methods on a chain of returned objects. Instead: `user.getZip()`. Violations create tight coupling — changes to `Address` break `User`'s callers. 'Don't talk to strangers.'

questions.prompt: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) specifically means:
options: Never copy-paste code
Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation in the system
Use helper functions for any code over 3 lines
Abstract everything into reusable utilities
questions.explanation: DRY is about knowledge, not code. Two similar code snippets that represent different business rules are NOT DRY violations. Premature DRY abstraction (combining things that happen to look similar) creates wrong abstractions. The test: if you change the business rule, do you need to change it in exactly one place?

questions.prompt: When should you prefer a Factory Method over directly calling `new MyService()`?
options: Always — direct instantiation is always bad
When the type of object to create depends on context, configuration, or runtime conditions — the factory encapsulates that decision
Only in strongly typed languages
Only when using dependency injection frameworks
questions.explanation: If you `new SqlDatabase()` everywhere, switching to `MongoDatabase` requires finding every usage. A factory method/function centralises this decision. Also enables returning different subtypes, caching instances, or logging creation without touching call sites.

questions.prompt: In a React app, `React.memo`, `useMemo`, and `useCallback` all implement which structural pattern concept?
options: Decorator
Proxy — they intercept renders or function calls and return cached results if inputs haven't changed
Flyweight — sharing component instances
Facade — simplifying the React API
questions.explanation: These are memoization proxies: they intercept the render/call, check if inputs changed, and return the cached result if not. The wrapped component/function has no knowledge of this caching layer — classic transparent proxy.

questions.prompt: Event sourcing stores state as a sequence of events rather than current state. This relates to which design pattern?
options: Command + Memento: Commands produce Events (immutable records); replaying them from the Memento (initial state) reconstructs current state
Observer: events notify all subscribers
Strategy: different event handlers pick different strategies
State machine with event transitions
questions.explanation: Event sourcing = Command pattern (events are Commands that happened) + Memento (each event snapshot can restore state). Replaying events from a snapshot is fundamentally Memento restoration. CQRS systems use this extensively.

questions.prompt: Promise chaining in JavaScript (`.then().then().catch()`) most closely resembles which pattern?
options: Observer
Chain of Responsibility
Command
Iterator
questions.explanation: Each `.then()` handler is a link in the chain that either passes the result to the next handler or short-circuits into `.catch()`. This is Chain of Responsibility — each handler decides to process and pass, or stop the chain.

questions.prompt: YAGNI principle applied: a developer adds a `sortOrder` parameter to a list endpoint 'because we'll need it someday'. YAGNI says:
options: Add it — backwards compatibility is important
Don't add it — you aren't gonna need it yet. Build what's needed now; adding it later when actually required will cost less than maintaining unused code
Add it behind a feature flag
Discuss with the team first
questions.explanation: YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): premature features add maintenance burden, test surface, API surface, and documentation overhead — often for requirements that change or never materialise. Build what's required now; extend when the use case is confirmed.

questions.prompt: The difference between a Service Locator and Dependency Injection:
options: Service Locator: class pulls dependencies from a global registry (hidden coupling); DI: dependencies are pushed in via constructor/interface (explicit coupling)
Service Locator is always faster
DI requires a framework; Service Locator doesn't
They are architecturally equivalent
questions.explanation: Service Locator hides dependencies — looking at a class's constructor doesn't tell you what it needs. DI makes dependencies explicit in the constructor/interface. Service Locator is now considered an anti-pattern because it makes classes harder to test and reason about.

questions.prompt: Implement the Observer pattern in TypeScript with a generic `EventEmitter<T>` class supporting `on(event, callback)` and `emit(event, payload)`. Then explain how this differs from Node.js's built-in EventEmitter.

rubric.criterion: Uses Map<string, Set<Function>> or similar to store listeners per event
on() correctly adds listener to the event's set
emit() iterates and calls all listeners for that event
Generic type parameter T constrains the payload type
Explains Node EventEmitter lacks generics by default / needs typed-emitter

questions.prompt: Design a Builder for creating a complex `DatabaseQuery` object that supports: table name (required), where clauses (array), order by (optional), limit (optional). Show the fluent interface and explain why Builder is better than a config object parameter here.

rubric.criterion: Each method returns `this` for fluent chaining
Separate build() or execute() step that validates required fields
Required field (table) validated at build time, not silently ignored
Explains Builder advantage: compile-time method names vs stringly-typed config object
Handles optional fields correctly (not set = omitted from query)

questions.prompt: Explain the Strategy pattern and implement it in TypeScript: a `PaymentProcessor` that can use either `StripeStrategy` or `PayPalStrategy`. Show how you'd switch strategies at runtime and why this is better than if/else branching.

rubric.criterion: Defines IPaymentStrategy interface with processPayment(amount) method
PaymentProcessor holds a private reference to IPaymentStrategy
Concrete classes (StripeStrategy, PayPalStrategy) implement the interface
Explains OCP benefit: adding new payment provider = new class only, no modification to PaymentProcessor

questions.prompt: In a REST API, logging middleware that wraps every route handler — `logger(req, res, next) { log(req); next(); log(res); }` — implements which two patterns simultaneously?
options: Command + Observer
Decorator + Chain of Responsibility
Proxy + Factory
Facade + Singleton
questions.explanation: Decorator: wraps the route handler and adds logging behaviour without modifying the handler. Chain of Responsibility: the middleware chain passes the request through multiple handlers via `next()`. Express middleware is a canonical example of both patterns working together.

questions.prompt: A React component that fetches its own data, renders a form, validates input, and submits to an API violates SRP. The correct split is:
options: Keep it as one component — React components are allowed to have multiple concerns
Split into: useDataFetching hook (data), FormUI component (render), useFormValidation hook (validate), submitService (API call)
Split only if the component exceeds 200 lines
Use context to manage all concerns centrally
questions.explanation: SRP in React: each unit should have one reason to change. Data fetching logic should change when the API changes; rendering logic when design changes; validation when rules change. Hooks separate data/logic concerns; components handle rendering only.

questions.prompt: Tell-Don't-Ask principle: instead of `if (account.getBalance() > amount) { account.debit(amount) }`, prefer:
options: Keep the check in the caller — it's clearer
`account.debit(amount)` where Account internally checks balance and throws if insufficient — the object owns its own invariants
Use a Validator class to centralise all checks
Store balance as a public field for direct access
questions.explanation: Tell-Don't-Ask: tell objects what to do, don't ask for their state to make decisions for them. Objects should enforce their own invariants. When callers inspect internal state to make decisions, they're doing the object's job and create duplication of business rules.

questions.prompt: Abstract Factory is used when building a UI library that must support both Material and Cupertino (iOS) themes. Calling `const factory = getFactory('ios'); factory.createButton(); factory.createDialog()` ensures:
options: All components come from the same theme family — you can't accidentally mix Material buttons with Cupertino dialogs
Components are cached for performance
Components are lazy-loaded
Components share the same event bus
questions.explanation: Abstract Factory's key guarantee: product consistency within a family. The CupertinoFactory only produces Cupertino components; MaterialFactory only Material. Switching themes = swap the factory. You can't mix families accidentally.

questions.prompt: Given: multiple microservices each publishing events independently, and multiple consumers subscribing to relevant events. This is best described as:
options: Mediator — services communicate via a central broker
Observer — publishers and subscribers, but decoupled via a message broker (event bus)
Command — each event is a command
Both Mediator and Observer aspects are present
questions.explanation: Event-driven microservices use Observer semantics (publish/subscribe) but route via a broker (Kafka, SNS) which acts as a Mediator. Architecturally, it's Pub/Sub (Observer variant) with a message broker playing the Mediator role. This is commonly called Event-Driven Architecture.

questions.prompt: Explain when you would use a Proxy vs a Decorator. Give a real backend example of each (not a toy example).

rubric.criterion: Proxy: adds cross-cutting concern transparently — client code doesn't change (e.g., API client with automatic retry/circuit breaking)
Decorator: caller explicitly opts in — e.g., logging wrapper the caller wraps their function with knowingly
Proxy implements the exact same interface as the real object; client can't tell the difference
Decorator typically extends the interface or is explicitly composed by the caller

questions.prompt: Coupling vs cohesion: ideal code has:
options: High coupling, high cohesion
Low coupling, low cohesion
Low coupling, high cohesion
High coupling, low cohesion
questions.explanation: Low coupling: modules depend on each other as little as possible (easy to change one without breaking others). High cohesion: each module focuses on a single well-defined responsibility. These are the two fundamental forces in software design — maximize both simultaneously.
